name: Sardines / oily fish

lead: Sardines are small oily fish eaten fresh, grilled, smoked or canned, valued as an inexpensive source of protein, B12 and omega-3 fats. Some in appearance communities eat them for healthier-looking skin.

The route people point to is omega-3 intake lowering skin inflammation. Canned Pacific sardines provide 375 percent of the daily value of B12 per 100 grams and calcium when eaten with the bones. No clinical studies on sardines for skin were found in the sources reviewed.

paras: People eat canned sardines on toast, with rice or in salads, a few times a week as a budget protein. Canned fish is shelf-stable, which makes it easy to keep up.
Sardines are described as lower in mercury than many fish, and canned versions contain notable sodium. Pacific sardine fisheries have faced closures, which can affect supply.

angle.text: Sardines and other oily fish are eaten as a cheap source of omega-3 fats, B12 and protein, with users linking them to healthier-looking skin through lower inflammation. Omega-3 intake is widely studied for health; skin benefits from eating oily fish were not tested in the sources reviewed.

lead: Sardines are small, oily forage fish eaten fresh, grilled, smoked or canned. In appearance-focused diet discussion they are promoted as a source of omega-3 fatty acids said to benefit skin [1].

Canned Pacific sardines are notable for protein and vitamin B12, with 375 percent of the daily value per 100 grams, and provide calcium when eaten with bones [1]. The reference article gives no omega-3 quantities and cites no clinical studies on skin [1].
infobox: Not examined in the sources reviewed

paras: Per 100 grams, canned Pacific sardines provide about 185 kilocalories, 20.9 grams of protein and 10.4 grams of fat, plus B12, phosphorus, niacin, riboflavin, calcium, iron and zinc [1].

Because they sit low on the food chain, sardines are described as carrying less mercury than many other commonly eaten fish [1]. In April 2015 the Pacific Fishery Management Council halted the US West Coast commercial sardine season after stocks collapsed [1]. The IUCN lists the European pilchard as Least Concern [1].
Cornish pilchard fishing thrived from about 1750 to 1880, and the last large US sardine cannery closed in 2010 [1].
No studies found on sardines specifically for skin or appearance outcomes.
